title: Design and Fault Detection of Charge Pump PLLs with NAND Gate based PFD Using BPNN and PNN
authors: Ramesh J.; Govindaraj V.; Ezhilazhagan C.; Sharmila Devi S.
source: Circuits, Systems, and Signal Processing
abstract: The Phase-Locked Loop (PLL) is one of the fundamental building blocks of modern mixed-signal systems utilized across communication, control, and signal processing applications. One of the most significant challenges with performing conventional functional tests on PLLs is that performance can be affected due to permanent defects, as well as manufacturing process and environmental variances. In this paper, a relatively new method for detecting faults in Charge Pump (CP) PLLs using Back Propagation Neural Networks (BPNN) and Probabilistic Neural Networks (PNN) is presented. A dataset containing 7200 samples of transistor-level simulations of a CP-PLL using the different threshold voltages (Vth), oxide thicknesses (Tox), and temperatures is used in the development of the classifiers. Seven fault classes is defined for the CP-PLL: Fault-free (FF), Drain Open (DO), Source Open (SO), Drain to Source Short (DSS), Gate to Drain Short (GDS), Gate to Source Short (GSS), and Gate Open (GO). Data were divided into training and testing/validation. The test set included newly generated process and environmental variations that had not been seen previously and were used to assess the robustness of the trained classifiers. The experiments demonstrated that the suggested PNN classifier accomplished an overall fault classification accuracy of 99.6%, which included an average precision of 0.9965, average recall of 0.9965, and average F1-score of 0.9964, across all fault classes. Work was based on complete circuit-level simulation. Consequently, the developed framework for automated fault classification based on PNNs provides a cost-effective, accurate, and fast solution for automated PLL fault identification in mixed-signal integrated circuits. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

title: Design and implementation of multi-channel parallel automatic test platform for aerospace power control module
authors: H. Ma; M. Huang; Y. Ren
source: 4th International Conference on Data Analytics, Computing and Artificial Intelligence (ICDACAI 2025)
abstract: Aiming at the problems of low test efficiency, poor synchronization accuracy and insufficient automation degree of aerospace power control module, this paper designs and implements a highly reliable automation platform that supports more than 32 channels of parallel testing. The platform adopts a layered redundant architecture, with FPGA as the core to realize 5ns synchronous trigger, and combines dynamic delay compensation algorithm and real-time error evaluation model to ensure the testing accuracy of dynamic response. The multi-channel acceleration model is constructed, and the efficiency gain of quantitative test is 28.2 times. Integrated adaptive test engine, supporting automatic script generation, fault self-recovery and one-button report output, realizing closed-loop management of the whole process. Three-mode redundancy and anti-radiation reinforcement are introduced into the hardware of the platform, so that the failure rate of SEE (Single Event Effect) is reduced to 0.12 FIT (Failures In Time), and the error of key parameters in the range of −55 °C~+125 °C is controlled within 0.3% through the temperature drift compensation model. title: Diagnostic Test Generation for Fault Localization in Printed Neuromorphic Circuits
authors: Gheshlaghi T.; Studt A.; Pal P.; Moussa D.A.; Hefenbrock M.; Beigl M.; Tahoori M.B.
source: Proceedings -Design, Automation and Test in Europe, DATE
abstract: Printed electronics (PE) enable lightweight, flexible, and low-cost devices for the Internet of Things (IoT) and wearable applications. Compared to conventional silicon-based electronics, PE trades peak performance for advantages in cost efficiency, mechanical flexibility, and large-area fabrication. However, its manufacturing processes remain unreliable and are prone to structural defects and variation due to inherent limited control in additive manufacturing. Printed neuromorphic circuits (pNCs) leverage the benefits of PE for on-demand analog edge computation in target applications but remain vulnerable to such defects. Diagnostic testing is therefore essential not only for detection but also for localizing faults to specific subcircuits and regions in the layout, a step critical for guiding yield improvement and reducing the cost of downstream inspection. We propose a diagnostic test pattern generation (DTPG) framework for fault localization in pNCs under black-box access. While ATPG is typically formulated as an optimization problem for fault detection, our approach extends this formulation by explicitly optimizing for fault distinguishability. On ten UCI datasets, the framework achieves up to 20.7% higher diagnostic coverage with a reduction of up to 3.6 times the number of undetectable subcircuits than detection-only test sets, while constraining the number of patterns to reduce storage overhead. These results demonstrate effective fault localization and establish a foundation for finer-grained, component-level diagnosis in future work.  © 2026 EDAA.

title: Distributed Delay-Based BIST for Mixed-Signal Circuits in Flexible Electronics
authors: Duarte P.C.L.; Ozev S.; Tahoori M.
source: Proceedings of the European Test Workshop
abstract: Flexible electronics (FE) based on indium gallium zinc oxide thin-film transistors (IGZO-TFTs) are emerging for ultra-low-power wearable applications. However, lack of packaging, limited pins, and high device variability make conventional Automatic Test Equipment (ATE) impractical for testing analog/mixed-signal circuits in FE. This work presents a dualpurpose ring oscillator (RO) and voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) serving as functional timing blocks and core structures for a distributed delay-based BIST framework. The oscillators achieve 1100 × area reduction and 5600 × lower power than previous IGZO-TFT designs. Lightweight digital BIST embedded within each RO stage enables stage-wise delay monitoring for defect detection. The BIST achieves 93% defect coverage for individual defects and 88% for multiple simultaneous defects, with only 3% power overhead and no external test equipment. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Distributionally robust fairness-based last-mile relief network optimization with casualty uncertainty
authors: Yang G.; Yuan H.; Yang W.; Jia R.
source: Reliability Engineering and System Safety
abstract: The suddenness and the casualties’ uncertainty of natural disasters urgently require a fair and robust network design for the medical supply distribution and the injured evacuation to reduce their post-disaster impact. This study establishes a distributionally robust chance-constrained model for medical supplies allocation in last-mile relief networks, with the objective of minimizing the worst-case Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) of supply shortages. The distribution of severely injured casualties is characterized via a scenario-wise ambiguity set, thereby the proposed model is reformulated as a mixed-integer linear programming problem for tractability. Numerical experiment based on Wenchuan earthquake derives several important findings. First, total supplies and raw materials exhibit analogous effects—increasing either reduces shortage levels initially, but further reductions are constrained by the other factor; Second, in response to high risks, the tendency is to build additional medical stations rather than expanding the scale of existing ones to disperse risk. Conversely, when risk is low, scaling up existing medical stations is preferred over establishing temporary facilities; Finally, under out-of-sample data fluctuations, the CVaR model demonstrates stronger robustness than the sample average approximation model, with consistently smaller standard deviations and superior stability. title: Evaluating an Analog Test Pattern Generation Tool by Means of Hardware-Emulated Fault Injection
authors: Duarte L.A.; Zilch L.B.; Ferreira A.F.G.; Lubaszewski M.S.; Balen T.R.
source: Latin American Test Workshop, LATW
abstract: This work presents a hardware-emulated fault injection experiment designed to evaluate a previously proposed test pattern generation tool for analog circuits. The tool processes the SPICE netlist of the circuit under test, performing iterative fault simulations and analyzing AC, DC, and transient responses at internal nodes and primary outputs. Its output is a test sequence that identifies optimal stimuli and observation points to maximize fault coverage. For experimental validation, a simple operational amplifier was implemented using MOS transistors from a commercial device. The SPICE netlist and corresponding transistor models were provided as input to the tool. The generated test sequence was then applied to the hardware circuit while open and short faults were injected directly into the hardware, considering the same fault model which was previously simulated. Experimental results show good fault coverage and good agreement with the simulations. title: Fault Tolerant Design of IGZO-based Binary Search ADCs
authors: Duarte P.C.L.; Ozev S.; Tahoori M.
source: Proceedings - International Symposium on Quality Electronic Design, ISQED
abstract: Thin-film technologies such as Indium Gallium Zinc Oxide (IGZO) enable Flexible Electronics (FE) for emerging applications in wearable sensing, personal health monitoring, and large-area systems. Analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) serve as critical sensor interfaces in these systems. Yet, their vulnerability to manufacturing defects remains poorly understood despite unipolar technologies' inherently high defect densities and process variations compared to mature CMOS technologies. We present a hierarchical fault injection framework to characterize defect sensitivity in Binary Search ADCs implemented in n-type only technologies. Our methodology combines transistor-level defect characterization with system-level fault propagation analysis, enabling efficient exploration of both single and multiple fault scenarios across the conversion hierarchy. The framework identifies critical fault-sensitive circuit components and enables selective redundancy strategies targeting only the most sensitive components. The resulting defect-tolerant designs improve fault coverage from 60% to 92% under single-fault injections and from 34% to 77.6% under multi-fault injection, while incurring only 4.2% area overhead and 6% power increase. While validated on IGZO-TFTs, the methodology applies to all emerging unipolar technologies.  © 2026 IEEE.

title: Fractal-Guided Circuit Testing Algorithm for Efficient Mixed-Signal VLSI Verification and Validation
authors: Anbazhagan L.; Senthilkumar S.
source: Proceedings of the 2026 13th International Conference on Computing for Sustainable Global Development, INDIACom 2026
abstract: Mixed-signal Very Large-Scale Integration (VLSI) circuits involving a combination of analog and digital components are encountering growing verification and validation problems because of complicated interactions, process variability and nonlinearities. The available methods of testing are time-consuming, they do not cover as many faults as possible, and they do not always analyze the most important components of the circuit in detail. The current study introduces a new Fractal-Guided Adaptive Resonance Testing (FGART) model that is the first model to combine the multi-scale fractal-based test vector generation with the adaptive resonance-based fault detection in mixed-signal VLSI verification. FGART quickly concentrates the testing on risky circuits areas and offers far superior coverage of faults compared to deterministic, random, or fractal-only approaches and uses less time and power. Multi-scale test vectors produced by FGART are based on fractal inspired metrics and it also adapts dynamically to the resonance patterns of the circuit by changing the test intensity. This is a good way of facilitating concentration of testing resources in regions that are high risk. This hybrid method will guarantee that the behaviour of analog and digital components are both exercised efficiently, with no extra simulations of duplicate responses, and subtle parametric and functional faults are targeted. Testing of FGART on standard mixed-signal benchmarks indicates a total test-time reduction of 40 percent and a 22 percent improvement in fault coverage compared to the classical random, deterministic, and fractal-only test cases. Moreover, FGART is highly scalable to larger and more complex VLSI designs whilst remaining efficient with an increase in the complexity of the circuit. To conclude, FGART is an innovative, intelligent, adaptive, framework of mixed-signal VLSI verification and validation; it is capable of being fast, reliable, and less abstraction among its computational requirements, and offers future avenues to improved automated testing solutions. title: Graph-Based Efficient Generation of Cell-Aware Models for Structural SRAM Testing
authors: Mongelli G.; Ronga D.; Faehnm E.; Girard P.; Virazel A.
source: IEEE Transactions on Device and Materials Reliability
abstract: Testing advanced memories is critical for ensuring SoC quality, especially as smaller transistors increase manufacturing defects occurrence, making traditional SRAM functional testing insufficient. To address this issue, a novel structural testing approach based on the Cell-Aware test methodology has been proposed. Structural test patterns are generated by an Automatic Test Pattern Generator (ATPG) using analog CA models, which are derived from exhaustive analog simulations of SRAM primary blocks. However, generating these CA models through analog simulations is both time-consuming and technology-dependent. To overcome this limitation, the TrUnDeL methodology was developed to accelerate CA model generation by combining switch-level graph-based analysis with analog simulations. In this work, we further adapt TrUnDeL to generate CA models solely through switch-level graph-based simulations, completely eliminating the need for analog simulations. The resulting TrUnDeL CA models are then used by the ATPG to create structural test patterns. Through a validation flow, we demonstrate that these patterns, generated without any analog simulations, achieve nearly the same fault coverage as those produced using exhaustive analog simulations in an SRAM case study. Furthermore, the CA model generation time is drastically reduced from one hour to just fifteen seconds for the same case. © 2001-2011 IEEE.

abstract: This article presents hardware-efficient harmonics cancellation techniques using digital predistortion (DPD) for low-distortion sinusoidal signal generation, targeted for the dynamic characteristic testing of high-resolution 14-bit and 16-bit 1 MS/s analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) in VLSI testing environments. The parameters are extracted via a single-step, deterministic calibration flow, ensuring high testing throughput without iterative optimization. Experimental results show HD2-HD5 levels down to -120 dBc, providing a hardware-efficient solution for high-precision built-out self-test (BOST) and future system-on-chip (SoC) integration.  © 1993-2012 IEEE.

title: High-Accuracy, Low-Utilization Multichannel 2-ps Bin Size FPGA Digital-to-Time Converter Based on Compact Multidimensional Delay Array
authors: Chen P.; Wijaya J.A.; Chen C.; Wen X.; Holst S.

abstract: Digital-to-time converter (DTC) or digital delay/timing generator has been developed for quite many years and plays a crucial role in automatic test equipment (ATE) and built-in self-test (BIST) industries. This study proposes a compact multidimensional delay array DTC based on phase shift in a phase-locked loop (PLL) to further extend field-programmable gate array (FPGA) applications into the analog domain. All internal delay cells are precisely controlled by PLL from the beginning to make the output phases distributed within the reference clock period as uniformly as possible. For further resolution enhancement, a hybrid structure based on PLL and a multidimensional delay array is presented to ensure high enough accuracy and substantially reduce logic utilization through phase sorting and selection. abstract: This paper presents a low-cost and fully digital framework for generating high-purity multitone waveforms using only a 7-bit-matched DAC and a 14-bit ADC, where the ADC serves both as the device under test and as the measurement instrument for co-testing. title: High-Resolution Broadband Coprime Spectrum Sensing System Based on Single TI-ADC Digital Synthesis
authors: Liu F.; Zang C.
source: 2026 5th International Symposium on Aerospace Engineering and Systems, ISAES 2026
abstract: Broadband spectrum surveillance today is constrained by prohibitive sampling-rate demands and intricate hardware stacks. Conventional coprime sampling schemes built on dual-ADC arrays break the Nyquist barrier but are plagued by sub-picosecond clock skew, inflexible frequency resolution, and poor statistical robustness - drawbacks that undermine their utility in volatile electromagnetic scenarios. To address these limits, this work develops a single-ADC coprime undersampling framework with digital-domain stream splitting: a 16 Gsps time-interleaved ADC executes full-rate direct RF sampling, after which an FPGA-embedded polyphase decimation filter derives two coprime subsequences from the identical high-speed data flow. This design reframes physical synchronization challenges as deterministic digital delays, eradicating the clock-alignment defects inherent to dual-ADC topologies. We further incorporate a block expansion factor and overlap ratio to prolong the effective autocorrelation lag span, enabling software-tunable resolution across 900 Hz-16 MHz; overlap segmentation concurrently mitigates the statistical variance induced by block stretching. Deployed on a dual Xilinx XCKU FPGA platform, the system delivers 200 MHz instantaneous bandwidth and 900 Hz resolution across 30 MHz-6 GHz. The proposed architecture offers a low-cost, agile engineering pathway for broadband RF sensing.  © 2026 IEEE.

title: IABIST: An IJTAG-Compliant Machine Learning-Based Analog BIST Framework for SoC Verification
authors: Kouamo J.; Simeu E.; Portolan M.
source: Proceedings of the IEEE VLSI Test Symposium
abstract: In modern SoC architectures, analog and digital blocks coexist intimately, yet their test methodologies remain largely disjoint. While digital testing has matured through standards such as IEEE 1149, 1500, and 1687, analog testing still lacks a unified framework. The main reason for this lack of synergy is the intrinsic interactive nature of analog testing, while digital testing is largely static. This paper introduces IABIST (Integrated IJTAG-Analog BIST), an architecture that merges analog Built-In Self Test with the interactive capabilities of IJTAG (IEEE 1687). By encapsulating analog modules within an ICL-described 'black-box' wrapper and leveraging PDL-driven orchestration, IABIST provides a single digital access point to stimulate and analyze both analog and digital domains. Within this unified test network, an on-chip analog stimulus generator excites the circuit, and a machine-learning-based response analyzer classifies its behavior. We present the complete co-simulation flow involving ModelSim, Cadence, and MAST, demonstrate IJTAG command mapping to analog actions, and validate the feasibility of analog test automation through ML inference. The results show that IABIST enables scalable, automated and fully retargetable SoC test operations. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Innovative Practices Session: Applying Analog Scan to Industrial Circuits
authors: Sunter S.; Saikiran M.; Chen D.; Mathur A.
source: Proceedings of the IEEE VLSI Test Symposium
abstract: Digital scan-based design-for-test (DfT) and automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) are widely used for testing random logic in ICs and routinely achieve $\gt 95 \%$ stuck-at fault coverage. Analog and mixed-signal (AMS) circuits are mostly treated as black-boxes and end up having unknown defect coverage and ad hoc DfT. Typically, AMS circuit blocks are addressed by specification-based tests for which analog defect simulation times would take hours, days, or longer, if they are run at all. The new IEEE 2427 standard [1] defines how to measure analog defect coverage but does not provide ways to reduce defect simulation time. Building on two published analog structural DfT techniques [2][3], a general digital scan-based DfT technique and ATPG were recently described [4] for which >95% coverage of opens and shorts in ‘random analog’ circuits was achieved in defect simulation times $\lt 1$ hour and test times $\lt 1 \mathrm{~ms}$. This was later extended to a 10-bit R-2R DAC [5].

title: Integrating Standardized Defect Modeling and Machine Learning for Alternative Testing of AMS Circuits
authors: Kouamo J.; Simeu E.; Portolan M.
source: 2026 International Conference on Control, Automation and Diagnosis, ICCAD 2026
abstract: The increasing complexity of Analog and Mixed-Signal (AMS) integrated circuits makes conventional specification-based testing costly and time-consuming, motivating the development of efficient alternative test methodologies. This paper presents a machine learning (ML) framework for AMS circuit testing aligned with the IEEE 2427-2025 standard for analog defect modeling. The proposed approach constructs a comprehensive defect universe combining stochastic parametric process variations and structural hard defects injected at the netlist level. These circuits are stimulated using broadband excitation signals, specifically Amplitude-Modulated Pseudo-Random Multi-Level Sequences (APRMLS), to enable the extraction of information-rich transient signatures. A Random Forest classifier is then trained using a hybrid labeling strategy that integrates specification compliance, functional monitoring, and structural defect knowledge to minimize test escapes. The methodology is validated on various AMS benchmark circuits, including an operational amplifier and a bandgap voltage reference. Experimental results demonstrate high defect detection capability and robustness across process variations without requiring intrusive Design-for-Test (DfT) hardware. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Loopback Built-in Self-Test for the UCIe Interface
authors: Persicke A.; Scholze S.; Wagner T.
source: 2026 International Conference on IC Design and Technology, ICICDT 2026
abstract: The Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) standard enables interoperable die-To-die communication for chiplet-based systems across a wide range of packaging technologies. As chiplet integration increasingly relies on advanced packaging, the economic impact of defective dies entering a package becomes substantial, since a single faulty chiplet can result in the costly loss of an entire multi-die assembly. Consequently, comprehensive wafer-level testing prior to packaging is a key requirement for chiplet-based systems-including the UCIe interface.Motivated by these constraints, this paper presents a loopback-based built-in self-Test (BIST) architecture targeting the analog front-end of the UCIe interface. The proposed approach enables at-speed wafer-level testing without reliance on high-performance external test equipment. By leveraging internal loopback configurations, the BIST supports standard high-speed I/O test methods, including bit error rate measurements, timing and voltage margining, data eye mask evaluation, and equalizer testing. Finally, a reference implementation is presented as a proof of concept.  © 2026 IEEE.

title: Optimal DfT test-transistor insertion for neural-network-classification-boosted latent pinhole detection and monitoring in Analog circuits
authors: Bhattacharya S.; Gielen G.
source: AEU - International Journal of Electronics and Communications
abstract: Latent defects, such as pinholes in the gate oxide of transistors, often escape through production tests but get activated while in the field. This paper presents a scalable defect-oriented Design for Testability (DFT) scheme that inserts extra test transistors in the analog circuit under test to allow extra current measurements from internal circuit nodes. Pinhole defect detection is then performed by feeding the measurements to a neural-network-based classifier. The minimum number and optimal locations of the test transistors in the circuit are determined through simulated annealing at design time. The approach is demonstrated in a 40-nm CMOS technology for two opamp circuits. The study demonstrates the potential to achieve more than 90% of detection coverage for pinhole defects with an electrical equivalent of more than 15% degradation in gate oxide thickness i.e. less than 85% effective gate oxide thickness. This work considers variations in process, transistor mismatch, and supply voltage, as well as the impact of the finite current sensor resolution. The circuits and area requirements for implementing the method in a BIST scheme for latent defect detection and in field monitoring in larger mixed-signal ICs are discussed. © 2026

title: PVTVAD: PVT-Variation-Aware Fault Diagnosis in ReRAM-based CAM Arrays
authors: Hezayyin H.G.; Mayahinia M.; Tahoori M.
source: IEEE Transactions on Device and Materials Reliability
abstract: Content Addressable Memories (CAMs) enable fast pattern matching and are widely used in modern systems. ReRAM-based CAMs (ReCAMs) offer high density, low power, and non-volatility; however, the interaction between intrinsic ReRAM defects and CMOS process variations introduces complex faulty behaviors that challenge conventional diagnosis. Moreover, ReCAM arrays are highly susceptible to process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) variations, whose impact is amplified in computation-in-memory (CiM) architectures due to analog sensing. Accurately localizing faulty cells in ReCAMs is particularly challenging because all cells in a row share the same match-line (ML), while only small ML voltage differences reveal location-dependent fault behavior. This paper presents a variation-aware Design-for-Testability (DfT) framework for precise ReCAM fault localization. The proposed DfT circuitry combines a tunable OpAmp and ADC with an iterative diagnosis flow that adaptively adjusts gain and sampling time in a multi-step process to improve diagnostic resolution under PVT variation. Results show that favorable voltage and temperature operating points can be exploited to accelerate diagnosis and reduce sensing overhead, while a partitioning-based diagnosis strategy reduces required gain by approximately 80% for large arrays. Across diverse fault scenarios and PVT corners, the proposed method localizes faults in only 2–8 diagnosis iterations and achieves approximately 2.29× lower diagnostic latency than March-based approaches, while incurring only 0.36% area overhead and up to 6.3% test-power overhead. © 2001 IEEE.

title: Reliable Emerging Electronics in Wearable and Implantable Healthcare Applications
authors: Pal P.; Duarte P.C.L.; Kashyap S.K.; Tahoori M.B.; Smith C.J.; Jung Y.; Gulick D.; Blain J.; Ozev S.
source: Proceedings of the IEEE VLSI Test Symposium
abstract: Flexible electronics (FE) are enabling a new generation of wearable and implantable healthcare systems; however, ensuring reliable operation remains challenging due to process variability, mechanical deformation, and harsh physiological environments. In implantable settings, long-term exposure to bodily fluids and pressure variations accelerates device degradation, while strict constraints on power and integration make the use of batteries and active electronics undesirable. This work presents a cross-layer approach to reliability in flexible healthcare systems by combining passive implantable sensing with robust wearable electronics. At the circuit level, we introduce ReFlex-LDO, a gainboosted IGZO-TFT low-dropout regulator designed for capacitorlight operation and integrated with a structural delay-based built-in self-test (BIST) scheme, achieving ∼ 95% fault coverage with minimal overhead. For signal acquisition, we develop a hierarchical fault modeling and mitigation framework for IGZObased Flash ADCs, enabling up to 98% single-fault and 91% multi-fault coverage through targeted design enhancements. At the system level, we propose a passive RF-based sensing mechanism for monitoring fluid flow in implantable biomedical devices, eliminating the need for on-board power and improving long-term reliability. By pairing passive implantable sensing elements with flexible wearable processing units, the proposed approach enables continuous health monitoring while mitigating risks associated with device degradation in the body. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Scalable Multi-Site Test Architecture for Chiplet-Based Systems on ATE Platforms
authors: Shin J.H.; Kim H.; Hwan Park J.; Lee Y.-W.
source: IEEE Transactions on Semiconductor Manufacturing
abstract: As chiplet technologies such as 2.5D/3D rapidly advance, chiplet testing approaches are becoming increasingly challenging. Specifically, stacking multiple chips or high bandwidth memory (HBM) in a single package increases the I/O pin count, leading to longer test times and multi-site test performance degradation due to increased test complexity and resource constraints. In turn, this results in higher testing costs as additional time and equipment are required to maintain test efficiency. In this paper, we propose a novel test interface integrating digital and analog compression modules to achieve high parallelism and precise fault detection. The proposed architecture incorporates a device under test (DUT) off masking sequence and a fault detection scheme, which enhances production efficiency while optimizing limited test resources by reusing analog test instruments that were not previously used in digital functional testing. This approach reduces overall test resource requirements and supports cost-effective parallel testing without additional equipment. Experimental results include an analysis of the architecture’s operational reliability under process variations and demonstrate a reduction in test resources and an average 82.2% decrease in test data volume on the ISCAS’89 and OpenCores benchmarks compared to prior work. © 1988-2012 IEEE.

title: SEAL: Multitenant Security-Aware Layer Mapping for Heterogeneous 3-D CiM Accelerators
authors: P. Sharma; S. P. Ramanujam; A. R. Bommana; H. Pourmehrani; N. Karimi; F. Firouzi; K. Chakrabarty
source: IEEE Journal on Exploratory Solid-State Computational Devices and Circuits
abstract: Heterogeneous 3-D compute-in-memory (CiM) architectures have emerged as an efficient acceleration paradigm for deep neural network (DNN) inference by leveraging the complementary characteristics of diverse memory technologies enabled through 3-D integration. Prior work has focused on architectural efficiency and workload-mapping optimization, leaving the security implications of heterogeneous CiM systems largely unexplored. This gap becomes critical in multitenant deployments, where the shared power delivery network (PDN) exposes the system to a ground-bounce-driven fault-injection attack: a malicious co-tenant drives switching-intensive activity that shifts the victim chiplet’s ground reference, corrupting memory reads during inference and degrading output quality. We propose SEAL, a security-aware layer-mapping framework that co-optimizes power, performance, area (PPA), and fault vulnerability across the layer-to-tier search space. SEAL combines per-layer criticality with device-level fault sensitivity to route vulnerability-critical layers to fault-resilient (device, tier) combinations, and we report the power and area of every mapping we present. We evaluate SEAL on ResNet-18 (CIFAR-10) and Qwen2.5-3B (WikiText-2) under attacker-induced ground bounce. SEAL reduces fault vulnerability by up to  $3.9\times $  on ResNet-18 and  $7.8\times $  on Qwen2.5-3B over a security-blind mapping baseline on compositions where both methods find usable mappings. On ReRAM-heavy compositions, SEAL places every high-criticality layer on a low-vulnerability tier and drives fault vulnerability to the characterization floor, an operating point the security-blind baseline does not reach. Accuracy stays within 0.06 pp of the fault-free baseline on ResNet-18 and perplexity within 0.06 of the fault-free baseline on Qwen2.5-3B. SEAL further finds usable mappings on three compositions (two on ResNet-18 and one on Qwen2.5-3B) where the security-blind baseline finds none.

title: SPOT IP Faults: Identifying Intermittent and Parametric Faults in Analog Circuits via Beluga Whale Optimization Driven Graph Attention Capsule Network
authors: Dhamotharan A.; Srinivasan K.
source: Journal of Circuits, Systems and Computers
abstract: Analog circuits within the core of electronic systems can introduce faults in the Circuit Under Test (CUT), which may lead to malfunction or even catastrophic failures. The intermittent and parametric faults are also quite hard to observe because of their random nature and non-reproducibility. In this research, a novel SPOT-IP fault detection model has been proposed to enhance the reliability and safety of an electronic system in the event of analog circuits. Initially, the Equispaced curvelet transform(N-ECT) is used to extract spectral, statistical characteristics from gathered signals containing the frequency response to enhance the localization of features. The proposed method utilizes a Graph Attention Capsule Neural Network (GACNN) that is used to categorize analog circuits as fault-free, parametric fault, and intermittent fault, using extracted features. Additionally, the hyperparameters of the GACNN are optimized using Beluga Whale Optimization to improve detection accuracy. The simulation was validated by the two ¯lters, namely the Sallen-Key bypass ¯lter (SK-BPF), and a Tow-Thomas ¯lter (TTF), and the proposed method is evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity and computational time. The proposed technique exhibits better accuracy for intermittent fault (99.12%) and parametric fault (99.25%) detection which is high compared to the existing techniques. © World Scientific Publishing Company

title: Structural Testing Methodology for Deep Neural Networks based on RRAM
authors: Serlis E.A.; Arapidis E.; Spyrou T.; Gebregiorgis A.; Taouil M.; Hamdioui S.; Fieback M.
source: Proceedings of the European Test Workshop
abstract: RRAM-based compute-in-memory (CIM) AI accelerators integrate memory cells with mixed-signal peripherals to enable energy-efficient, low-latency edge computing. These architectures require novel test techniques for unique electrical defects. Current system-level functional tests cannot guarantee defect-free circuits, while accurate circuit-level techniques remain non-scalable to Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). To bridge this gap, we present the first structural test methodology for CIM DNNs, unifying system-level analysis with circuit-level precision. We accurately model RRAM crossbar defects to formulate test patterns, and then propagate results across layers for comprehensive structural testing. Generated test patterns are optimized either for 96% defect coverage or test time reduction by a factor of three while covering all unique defects and maintaining over 73% defect strength coverage. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Testing of a 12 bit SARA and Cand Analog Scan

abstract: This paper presents results for the first silicon implementation of analog scan-based design-for-test (DfT) and automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) for an industrial mixed-signal circuit, a 12-bit SAR ADC in a 65 nm technology. The method allows generating a digital-only IJTAG test pattern and simulating to measure its defect coverage in a day, versus weeks for a ramp-based specification test. The DfT consists of an IJTAG test data register (TDR), digital multiplexers, analog stimulus transistors, and analog scan inverters, to control and observe ports of the ADC and nodes deep inside it. The DfT had minimal impact on the ADC's performance. The analog scan results were stable across multiple process corners, supply voltages, and stimulus frequencies, and high coverage testing of defect-free and intentionally defective devices was achieved in sub-millisecond test times. The paper discusses lessons learned, unexpected benefits, challenges identified, and future solutions. © 2026 IEEE.

authors: S. Chakri; N. Mouhni; F. Ennaama
source: 2026 International Conference on Circuit, Systems and Communication (ICCSC)
abstract: Predictive maintenance of metro rolling stock is constrained by the scarcity of labeled failure data. This paper proposes an unsupervised framework for the Air Production Unit (APU) of metro trains, combining a Variational Autoencoder with K-means clustering in a two-dimensional latent space. A dual-criterion scoring rule flags rare micro-clusters and points beyond the 97th percentile of intra-cluster centroid distance. Thresholds are calibrated on a failure-free validation period, kept strictly separate from the test set. On the MetroPT-3 dataset (1.51 M records, 1 Hz, Porto metro, February-August 2020), the method flags 4.6% of test samples and reaches a precision of 0.78, a recall of 0.86 and an F1 of 0.82, outperforming Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, a deterministic autoencoder and a reconstruction-only VAE by 0.08 to 0.21F1 points. title: Using Analog IJTAG to Measure ISO 26262 Metrics
authors: Praselski B.; Sunter S.
source: Proceedings of the European Test Workshop
abstract: The proposed P1687.2 analog extension to the widely used IEEE 1687 'IJTAG' standard for specifying digital IC tests and test access can greatly simplify writing production tests. This paper shows how the test language can support automated measurement of an analog circuit's ISO 26262 functional safety (FuSa) metrics by an analog fault simulator. The Latent Fault Metric (LFM) is the percentage of faults in a safety mechanism (e.g., voltage monitor) that prevent detecting a second fault occurring in monitored circuit; it is challenging to measure because fault simulators typically simulate only one fault at a time. A two-step solution to this limitation is described that is safer and more efficient than simulating two faults at a time. The resulting design-for-test (DfT) and test methods are also suitable for production testing of the circuit. Simulated results for an automatically generated SPICE testbench for a commonly used circuit are provided - a bandgap voltage source supplying a voltage regulator monitored by two comparators connected to a second bandgap. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Using Hardware-Emulated Fault Injection on the Evaluation of a Mixed-Signal Test Pattern Generation Tool
authors: L. A. Duarte; L. B. Zilch; Á. F. G. Ferreira; M. S. Lubaszewski; T. R. Balen

abstract: This paper presents a Hardware-Emulated Fault Injection framework for evaluating a previously proposed test pattern generation tool for mixed-signal circuits. Operating directly on the SPICE netlist of the circuit under test (CUT), the computational tool conducts successive fault simulations to evaluate the DC, AC, and transient behaviors across internal nodes and external outputs. It then produces a test sequence that identifies optimal stimuli and observation points to maximize fault coverage. For experimental validation, a simple operational amplifier and a StrongARM comparator were implemented using MOS transistors of a commercial device. The SPICE netlist and corresponding transistor models were provided as inputs to the tool. The generated test sequence was then applied to both physical circuits with open and short faults injected into the hardware, considering the same previously simulated fault model. Experimental results show good fault coverage and good agreement with the simulations. By considering as case studies a pure analog linear circuit and a non-linear, clocked, mixed-signal (MS) block, the feasibility of applying the tool to different kinds of MS devices is demonstrated.

authors: T. Gao; Y. Li; J. Yang; X. Fan
source: 2026 IEEE International Instrumentation and Measurement Technology Conference (I2MTC)
abstract: Analog circuits play an irreplaceable role in key fields such as intelligent transportation, and they are prone to intermittent faults (IFs), which pose a serious threat to system safety. This paper proposes a zero-shot meta-model for waveform segmentation (ZMWS), which constructs a single meta-prompt self-supervised meta-training framework. Without relying on actual fault datasets, the meta-model completes meta-training by learning the generic variation patterns from synthetic waveform sample pairs. A temporal feature alignment module is designed to address the phase variation issue between prompt samples and query samples. Meanwhile, the model adopts a one-dimensional DenseNet as the pre-trained encoder, integrating classification and denoising multi-tasks. It combines this encoder with a Dense-UNet decoder to innovatively achieve accurate segmentation of fault regions. Experimental results show that the ZMWS metamodel can realize zero-shot fault detection in meta-inference with only a single normal sample as the meta-prompt, achieving a fault detection rate of 97.7%. This method provides a new paradigm for the accurate localization of the occurrence time of intermittent faults in analog circuits under sample-scarce scenarios.

authors: Liu H.-C.H.; Soma M.
source: Proceedings - Pacific Rim International Symposium on Fault Tolerant Systems, RFTS 1991
abstract: A new approach to the fault diagnosis for analog integrated circuits is proposed. It uses fault models from the defect statistics to generate faulty circuits. Fault simulations are then applied to those faulty circuits to generate different fault classes which can be used for the fault diagnosis for analog integrated circuits. An example is also given to demonstrate this new approach. © 1991 IEEE.
keywords: Analog integrated circuits; Failure analysis; Fault tolerance; Fault tolerant computer systems; Integrated circuit layout; Timing circuits; Defect statistics; Fault class; Fault model; Fault simulation; Faulty circuits; New approaches; Fault detection

title: Transient Analysis and Sensitivity Computation in Piecewise-Linear Circuits
authors: Elcherif Y.; Lin P.-M.
source: IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems
abstract: Basic relations are given for transient sensitivity computation of piecewise-linear (PWL) circuits modeled by ideal diodes. ? method is presented for computer-aided formulation and solution of the PWL transient sensitivity analysis problem using the adjoint network approach. An iterative complementary pivot algorithm is used for solving the original network equations, while the solution of the adjoint network equations is obtained without iterating. In the original network simulation, the iterations of the algorithm have to be performed only for a small subset of the total simulation time instants. © 1991 IEEE
keywords: Computer Simulation; Mathematical Techniques - Piecewise Linear Techniques; Mathematical Techniques - Sensitivity Analysis; Adjoint Network Method; Ideal Diodes; Piecewise Linear Circuits; Transient Sensitivity; Electric Networks, Nonlinear

title: Use of modified nodal analysis to write multiport hybrid matrix
authors: Augusto J.A.S.; Almeida C.F.B.
source: Electronics Letters
abstract: The n-port hybrid matrix is often used in practical problems such as solving nonlinear networks, writing state equations and writing fault diagnosis equations. A simple method to obtain the hybrid matrix based on the modified nodal analysis (MNA) circuit equations is described. This method is extremely suitable for computer implementation. © 1991 The Institution of Electrical Engineers. All rights reserved.

title: Built-in Self-Test (BIST) Structures for Analog Circuit Fault Diagnosis with Current Test Data
authors: Wey C.-L.; Krishnan S.
source: IEEE Transactions on Instrumentation and Measurement
abstract: In order to increase the number of test points, while still keeping low pin overhead, a built-in self-test (BIST) structure has been proposed for analog circuit fault diagnosis with voltage test data. This paper presents alternative BIST structures for fault diagnosis with current test data using current copiers. The current copiers make a practically identical copy of the current without the need of well-matched components. Thus, the proposed BIST structure requires less chip area. The proposed structure allows simultaneous sampling of current test data at various test points and shifting of the data to the output portion for fault diagnosis. Results have also shown that the proposed BIST structure is fully testable. © 1992 IEEE
keywords: Analog computers; Integrated circuit testing; Networks (circuits); Sampling; Analog circuits; Built in self test; Fault diagnosis; Automatic testing

title: Challenges in testing of mixed mode analog/digital ICs
authors: Maly W.
source: European Solid-State Circuits Conference
abstract: Testing of digital and analog ICs has became an extremely complex and often expensive activity. Testing of mixed digital/analog ICs is even more complex because of an interaction between two different environments - digital and analog - generating new failure modes. This paper examines - from a testing standpoint - basic characteristics of mixed digital/analog ICs. Out of the presented examination a possible new testing scenario, suitable for mixed ICs, is derived. It is argued that new mixed IC testing strategies must be build based on DFT techniques and that concepts successful in the digital domain must be expanded to cover entire mixed digital/analog testing arena. © 1992 European Solid-State Circuits Conference.
keywords: Analog integrated circuits; Timing circuits; Basic characteristics; Digital domain; IC testing; Mixed mode; Digital integrated circuits

title: Fault dictionary approach for fault diagnosis of switched capacitor circuits
authors: Salama A.E.; Amer F.Z.
source: International Journal of Electronics
abstract: The fault dictionary approach has been found to be very useful for diagnosing switched capacitor circuits. In this paper we present the application of fault dictionary techniques for fault diagnosis of switched capacitor circuits using excitations in the time-domain. The nearest-neighbour rule criterion, and the concept of ambiguity sets are used for fault isolation under the effect of uncertainties due to element tolerances. © 1992 Taylor & Francis Ltd.
keywords: Capacitors--Applications; Computer Programming--Algorithms; Ambiguity Sets; Fault Diagnosis; Fault Dictionary; Nearest-Neighbor Rule Criterion; Switched Capacitor Circuits; Time-Domain Excitations; Electronic Circuits

title: Hierarchical fault modeling for analog and mixed-signal circuits
authors: Nagi N.; Abraham J.A.
source: Proceedings of the IEEE VLSI Test Symposium
abstract: Presents a comprehensive approach, based on functional error characterization, for modeling faults in analog and mixed-signal circuits. A case study based on a CMOS and an nMOS operational amplifier is discussed, and a full listing of derived behavioral fault models is presented. These fault models are then mapped to the faulty behavior at the macro-circuit level. © 1992 IEEE.
keywords: Electric signal systems; Operational amplifiers; Timing circuits; VLSI circuits; Analog and mixed signal circuits; Circuit levels; Fault model; Functional errors; Mixed signal integrated circuits

title: Some aspects of knowledge-based fault diagnosis in electronic devices
authors: Vaez-Ghaemi R.; Godbersen W.; Schwetlick H.; Filbert D.
source: Measurement
abstract: The computer-aided fault diagnosis of electronic devices requires the acquisition of different kinds of information - i e, for the diagnosis strategy, measurement tasks and documentation purposes. This paper describes the application of knowledge-based methodologies to support the acquisition process. Major points of consideration will be the application of an inductive learning method for the diagnosis strategy and the implementation of a PROLOG-based consultation system for the generation of measurement instrument settings. © 1992.
keywords: fault diagnosis in electronic devices; inductive learning algorithm; Knowledge-based system

title: A fault dictionary based expert system for failure diagnosis in a multiple-PCB environment
authors: Arslan T.S.; Bottaci L.; Taylor G.E.
source: Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: This paper describes a failure-diagnosis expert system for printed circuit boards which exploits functional test data. The data is output from automatic test equipment which is used to test every board subsequent to manufacture. The use of a conventional machine-learning technique produced only limited success due to the very large search space of failure reports. This also ruled out the use of a conventional knowledge-based approach. In addition, there was a requirement to track changes in printed circuit board design and manufacture which also ruled out a conventional knowledge-based approach. The investigations led to the development of a system which tracks changes by learning in a more restricted search space derived from the original space of reports. The system performs a diagnosis by matching a failure report with information about previously seen reports. The matching rules used are heuristic. The system uses basic circuit connectivity information in conjunction with the matching procedure to improve diagnostic performance, especially in cases where matching fails to identify a unique component. © 1993.
keywords: diagnosis; fault dictionary; PCB test

title: A review of testing methods for mixed-signal ICs
authors: Harvey R.J.A.; Bratt A.H.; Dorey A.P.
source: Microelectronics Journal
abstract: Recent developments in Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs), which contain analogue as well as digital components on-chip, has meant an upsurge of interest in the problems of testing. Much successful research has already been carried out in fault-testing digital ICs, but although several methods of analogue testing are being tried, no one coherent philosophy has yet been agreed upon. This paper contrasts and reports on currently favoured analogue testing methodologies, and includes a discussion, with reference to recent work undertaken by the authors, of the applicability of the power supply current monitoring technique. © 1993.
keywords: Analog storage; Mathematical models; Signal processing; VLSI circuits; Fault testing; Mixed signal integrated circuits; Testing methods; Integrated circuits

title: Neural networks for multiple fault diagnosis in analog circuits
authors: Fanni A.; Giua A.; Sandoli E.
source: Proceedings - IEEE International Symposium on Defect and Fault Tolerance in VLSI Systems
abstract: Fault diagnosis of analog circuits is a complex problem. The paper discusses how the features of neural networks of learning from examples and of generalizing may be used to solve this problem. In a detailed applicative example, we show how, given the voltages values in a set of test points, a network may be trained to recognize catastrophic single faults on a circuit part of a direct current motor drive. The network is then used to diagnose multiple faults on two and three components. In this case the network is generally able to detect at least one of the malfunctioning components, although less sharply than in the case of single faults. © 1993 IEEE.
keywords: Analog circuits; Electric motors; Complex problems; Direct current motors; Faults diagnosis; Learning from examples; Motor drive; Multiple faults; Multiple faults diagnosis; Neural-networks; Single fault; Test-points; Fault detection

title: Qualitative dynamic diagnosis of circuits
authors: Fanni A.; Diana P.; Giua A.; Perezzani M.
source: Artificial Intelligence for Engineering, Design, Analysis and Manufacturing
abstract: We describe ACDS, an automatic diagnostic system. ACDS is capable of diagnosing faults on analog circuits in dynamic conditions. The circuit's dynamic behavior is studied by means of a series of intrastate simulations during which the qualitative state of the circuit does not change. An acquistion board collects the value of a set of quantities corresponding to accessible test points. These measurements are converted into qualitative values and are used for two purposes: first, to determine the state of the circuit components; second, to trigger the diagnostic procedure whenever a discrepancy between observed and predicted behavior is found. The main difficulty in this phase of measurement interpretation is in obtaining meaningful numerical-qualitative data conversion for values of quantities approaching a boundary between two different qualitative intervals. System performance has been verified through a number of simulations, which have shown the proposed approach to be efficient both in terms of localized faults and of flexibility in adapting to different circuits. © 1993, Cambridge University Press. All rights reserved.

title: Cross-correlation between idd and vout signals for testing analogue circuits
authors: da Silva J.M.; Matos J.S.; Bell I.M.; Taylor G.E.
source: Electronics Letters
abstract: The cross-correlation between iDD and vout signals is addressed as a means for improving the testing of analogue circuits. Besides the higher testing confidence provided by mixed iDD/vout monitoring, a single unified test operation is performed instead of two separate operations. © 1995, IEE. All rights reserved.
keywords: Analogue circuits; Electric current measurement; Testing; Voltage measurement; Computer simulation; Correlation theory; Electric current measurement; Error detection; Fault tolerant computer systems; Measurement errors; Monitoring; Monte Carlo methods; Performance; Signal processing; Voltage measurement; Analogue circuits; Mixed-signal circuits; Power supply circuits

title: Automatic fault diagnosis method for resistive network using multiple excitations
authors: Kim D.S.; Seong P.H.
source: International Journal of Circuit Theory and Applications
abstract: In this paper we develop and present an improved resistive circuit fault diagnosis method, a type of simulation after test (SAT), for the location of multiple faults in linear network. In this method we suggest a condition of branch fault diagnosis for locating multiple faults which is based on multiple excitation. Our diagnostic method based on this condition has the major advantage that it removes the necessity to verify the existence of multiple fault combinations. We demonstrate this method by applying it to a resistive network.
keywords: Automatic testing; Computer simulation; Electric conductivity; Electric excitation; Error detection; Failure analysis; Fault diagnosis; Multiple excitation; Resistive network; Simulation after test; Circuit theory

title: Automating the diagnosis of analogue circuits - A tutorial
authors: Garrett C.; Maikowski L.; Thomas R.
source: International Journal of Electrical Engineering and Education
abstract: A tutorial study of automatic analogue fault diagnosis is presented. Major issues, namely observability, controllability and deduction are explained but then issues of tolerance and fault models peculiar to diagnosis of faults in analogue systems are discussed. A taxonomy of methods is followed by examples and 25 references.
keywords: Automation; Controllability; Electric fault currents; Mathematical models; Observability; Teaching; Analog circuits; Automatic fault diagnosis; Linear network analysis

title: Hierarchical fault modeling for linear analog circuits
authors: Nagi N.; Abraham J.A.
source: Analog Integrated Circuits and Signal Processing
abstract: This paper presents a hierarchical fault modeling approach for catastrophic as well as out-of-specification (parametric) faults in analog circuits. These include both, ac and dc faults in passive as well as active components. The fault models are based on functional error characterization. Case studies based on CMOS and nMOS operational amplifiers are discussed, and a full listing of derived behavioral fault models is presented. These fault models are then mapped to the faulty behavior at the macro-circuit level. Application of these fault models in an efficient fault simulator for analog circuits is also described. © 1996 Kluwer Academic Publishers.
keywords: CMOS integrated circuits; Computer simulation; Electric fault currents; Error analysis; Failure analysis; Hierarchical systems; Mathematical models; MOS devices; Network components; Operational amplifiers; Analog circuits; Error characterization; Hierarchical fault modeling; Linear integrated circuits

title: Selecting measurements to test the functional behavior of analog circuits
authors: Van Spaandonk J.; Kevenaar T.A.M.
source: Journal of Electronic Testing: Theory and Applications (JETTA)
abstract: This paper presents a method for functional testing of analog circuits, on the basis of circuit sensitivities. The approach selects the minimum number of measurements that allows a precise prediction of a circuit's functional behavior. A criterion is applied to this predicted behavior to determine if the circuit functions according to specifications. The presented method combines a matrix decomposition technique (the singular value decomposition) with an iterative algorithm to select measurements. The number of measurements is determined on the basis of the desired precision of the response prediction and the influence of random measurement errors. Examples demonstrate that the resulting method tests the functional circuit behavior with a high precision, even in the presence of large measurement errors. © 1996 Kluwer Academic Publishers.
keywords: Analogue circuits; Automatic testing; Circuit testing; Algorithms; Approximation theory; Automatic testing; Iterative methods; Linear integrated circuits; Matrix algebra; Measurement errors; Analog circuits; Functional testing; Matrix decomposition techniques; Integrated circuit testing

title: Signature analysis for fault detection of mixed-signal ICs based on dynamic power-supply current
authors: Argüelles J.; Bracho S.
source: Journal of Electronic Testing: Theory and Applications (JETTA)
abstract: In this paper we have investigated a unified and simultaneous fault detection method for mixed-signal integrated circuits. The method is based on the analysis of the power-supply current through the circuit under test. The analysis has been done paying attention to the dynamic behaviour of the power-supply current, in order to avoid measurement problems related to the large amount of quiescent current drop across many analog blocks. The analysis of the dynamic power-supply current entails certain problems related to the complexity of the measurement process, especially those due to the high speed of the current transients. These problems have been addressed by considering a design for test procedure based on the use of built-in dynamic current sensors. The goal of the design for test methodology proposed is to represent the Iddt through the mixed-signal IC under test by a digital signature. The paper presents some advantages of this approach such as a good tolerance to crosstalk noise and the need for only a conventional digital tester on the complete mixed-signal IC for fault detection. The analysis is illustrated with some test results. © 1996 Kluwer Academic Publishers.
keywords: Built-in current sensors; Design for test in mixed-signal IC; Mixed-signal IC testing; Electric currents; Electric power supplies to apparatus; Error detection; Failure analysis; Integrated circuit layout; Sensors; Spurious signal noise; Built in dynamic current sensors; Digital signature; Dynamic power supply current; Signature analysis; Integrated circuit testing

title: Supply current test of analogue and mixed signal circuits
authors: Bell I.M.; Spinks S.J.; Machado Da Silva J.
source: IEE Proceedings: Circuits, Devices and Systems
abstract: Supply current test is well established for digital CMOS circuits and the advantages of improved observability and reliability indication have prompted its use for analogue and mixed signal circuits. A short review of the literature on this subject is given. Fault simulation is used for the investigation of dynamic supply current test of a PLL, confirming existing results from smaller circuits that a combination of supply current and output voltage monitoring leads to higher fault coverage. In the paper, fault coverage is further improved, using crosscorrelation of the supply current and output signals, and the potential for BIST implementation of this technique is demonstrated using low resolution polarised crosscorrelation. Fault simulation is also performed on an analogue multiplier to investigate the effect of process parameter deviations on the supply current. The fault coverage is found to be improved by removing the DC component of the signal. Encouraging results are obtained from the application of supply current test techniques to a commercial mixed signal ASIC currently beyond the capabilities of analogue fault simulation, indicating that efforts at improving fault simulation in this area are worthwhile. The requirements for fault modelling and simulation to support supply current test are discussed and some initial results of accelerating this process using macromodelling are presented. © IEE, 1996.
keywords: Mixed signal ICs; Supply current test; Application specific integrated circuits; CMOS integrated circuits; Computer simulation; Correlation methods; Electric fault currents; Mixer circuits; Multiplying circuits; Phase locked loops; Analog circuits; Analog multiplier; Fault simulation; Supply current test; Integrated circuit testing

title: Robust Fault Diagnosis for Large-Scale Analog Circuits with Measurement Noises
authors: Sheu H.-T.; Chang Y.-H.
source: IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems I: Fundamental Theory and Applications
abstract: A hierarchical frequency-domain robust component failure detection (RCFD) scheme is proposed for the diagnosis of large-scale analog circuits with measurement noises based on the design of robust detection filters and robust residual thresholds. The robust residuals generated by the robust detection filters are employed to realize both fault isolation (FI) and component failure detection (CFD). A procedure for the design of robust detection filters is proposed and the associated rule for the selection of measurement variables is suggested. Furthermore, the effect of the measurement noises to the diagnostic result can be reduced by the proper design of residual thresholds, and the robustness of the diagnosis is enhanced. Finally, an example is illustrated to show the efficacy of the proposed method. © 1997 IEEE.
keywords: Design; Efficiency; Electric fault currents; Frequency domain analysis; Hierarchical systems; Robustness (control systems); Signal noise measurement; Analog circuits; Electric filters

title: Analog test design with IDD measurements for the detection of parametric and catastrophic faults
authors: Lindermeir W.M.; Vogels T.J.; Graeb H.E.
source: Proceedings -Design, Automation and Test in Europe, DATE
abstract: Earlier approaches dealt with the detection of catastrophic faults based on IDD monitoring. Consideration of the more subtle parametric faults and the ADC quantization noise, however, is essential for high-quality analog testing. The paper presents a new design method for analog test of parametric and catastrophic faults by IDD monitoring. ADC quantization noise is systematically considered throughout the method. Results prove its effectiveness. © 1998 IEEE.
keywords: Design for testability; Analog test; Analog testing; Catastrophic fault; Design method; Fault-based; High quality; Parametric fault; Quantization noise; Test designs; Fault detection

title: A Neural-Based Analog IC Parametric Fault Diagnostic System with Discriminant Simulation Sampling
authors: Wu A.
source: Journal of Testing and Evaluation
abstract: This article presents experimental results that show feedforward neural networks are well suited for analog IC parametric fault diagnosis. It describes a discriminant sampling method for analog IC parametric faults simulation for a neural-based diagnostic system to reduce the computational overhead of the neural network training phase. Analog circuit fault simulation has not achieved the same degree of success as its digital counterpart owing to the difficulty in modeling the more complex analog behavior. Analog circuit fault simulation does rely on time-consuming circuit simulations on a large number of sampled points subject to various process deviations to emulate the actual faulty conditions. The proposed algorithm uses an effective importance sampling strategy to capture the parametric acceptance boundaries of the circuit under test. It makes use of circuit simulations effectively to relate each circuit performance to the process disturbances and to establish response functions that are accurate at the transition boundaries of the acceptance region. With the proposed approach, simulation samples can be generated for fault simulations mostly at the boundaries of the acceptance region to institute the discriminant functions for parametric faults testing using a neural network approach. The proposed algorithm is more computationally effective when compared to the Monte Carlo method.
keywords: Analog circuit; Discriminant sampling method; Fault diagnosis; Fault simulation; Neural network; Parametric faults

title: Behavioral Level Noise Modeling and Jitter Simulation of Phase-Locked Loops with Faults Using VHDL-AMS
authors: Godambe N.J.; Shi C.-J.R.
source: Journal of Electronic Testing: Theory and Applications (JETTA)
abstract: It is important to predict noise at the early stages of a top-down design. In this paper, we propose a methodology to model phase noise or jitter, a key specification for phase-locked loops, using a mixed-signal hardware description language, and to simulate the effects of catastrophic faults on the phase jitter at the behavioral level. In contrast to existing approaches which either require dedicated noise simulators or postpone noise and fault simulation to the transistor level, we have successfully demonstrated that noise in a voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO), power supply noise, and their effects on the overall phase jitter within a faulty PLL can be modeled and simulated earlier on at the behavioral level. Our simulation results are consistent with experimentally-verified theoretical predictions.
keywords: Analog test; Behavioral fault modeling; Fault modeling; Fault simulation; Jitter; Noise; Computer simulation; Error detection; Mathematical models; Phase locked loops; Printed circuit testing; Spurious signal noise; Variable frequency oscillators; Analog testing; Behavioral level noise modeling; Computer testing

title: Efficient DC fault simulation of nonlinear analog circuits
authors: Tian M.W.; Shi C.-J.R.
source: Proceedings -Design, Automation and Test in Europe, DATE
abstract: This paper describes a method to improve the efficiency of nonlinear DC fault simulation. The method uses the Newton-Raphson algorithm to simulate each faulty circuit. The key idea is to order the given list of faults in such a way that the solution of previous faulty circuit can serve as a good initial point for the simulation of the next faulty circuit. To build a good ordering, one step Newton-Raphson iteration is performed for all the faulty circuits once, and the results are used to quantify how faulty circuits and the good circuit are close in their behaviors. With one-step Newton-Raphson iteration implemented by Householder's formula, the proposed method has virtually no overhead. Experimental results on a set of 36 MCNC benchmark circuits show an average speedup of 4.4 and as high as 15 over traditional stand-alone fault simulation. © 1998 IEEE.
keywords: Timing circuits; Benchmark circuit; Fault's simulations; Faulty circuits; Initial point; Newton-Raphson algorithm; NewtonRaphson iteration (NRI); Nonlinear analog circuits; Stand -alone; Newton-Raphson method

title: Analog circuit fault diagnosis based on noise measurement
authors: Dai Y.; Xu J.
source: Microelectronics Reliability
abstract: In this paper, an analog circuit fault diagnosis method using a noise measurement and analysis approach is suggested. Compared to the conventional circuit fault diagnoses methods, this method can discover hidden and early circuit fault caused by the device defects. Since circuit fault diagnosis is more difficult than device-defect detection, in this paper the circuit output noise calculation, the comparison between the normal and failure conditions and the circuit fault diagnosis method have been discussed. Finally, an example of an active filter circuit fault diagnosis has been given by using this method.
keywords: Electric fault currents; Electric filters; Spurious signal noise; Analog circuit fault diagnosis; Linear network analysis

title: Integrated design and test of mixed-signal circuits
authors: Engin N.; Kerkhoff H.G.; Tangelder R.J.W.T.; Speek H.
source: Journal of Electronic Testing: Theory and Applications (JETTA)
abstract: In this paper, the integration of design and test flows for mixed-signal circuits is discussed. The aim is to decrease test generation and debugging costs and time-to-market for the analogue blocks in mixed-signal circuits. A tool developed in order to automate the data sharing between design and test environments is described and the functionality of this tool is explained. The generation of a test plan consists of the selection of the separate test functions and addition of commands for control signal generation and tester routing. The usage of design data for each of these functions is explained and the tool is evaluated in the design and testing of a mixed-signal demonstrator circuit. Results from this experience are discussed.
keywords: Integrated circuit layout; Mixer circuits; Mixed-signal demonstrator circuits; Integrated circuit testing

title: Neural network diagnosis approach for analog circuits
authors: Fanni A.; Giua A.; Marchesi M.; Montisci A.
source: Applied Intelligence
abstract: This paper presents a neural network system for the diagnosis of analog circuits and shows how the performance of such a system can be affected by the choice of different techniques used by its submodules. In particular we discuss the influence of feature extraction techniques such as Fourier Transforms, Wavelets and Principal Component Analysis. The system uses several different power supplies and as many neural networks 'in parallel'. Two different algorithms that can be used to combine the candidate sets produced by each network are also presented. The system is capable of diagnosing multiple faults even if trained on single ones.
keywords: Algorithms; Computer aided diagnosis; Error detection; Fault tolerant computer systems; Feature extraction; Fourier transforms; Networks (circuits); Pattern recognition systems; Wavelet transforms; Analog circuits; Deviation faults; Multiple fault diagnosis; Offline diagnosis; Online diagnosis; Principal component analysis; Neural networks

title: Optimized statistical analog fault simulation
authors: Khouas Abdelhakim; Dessouky Mohamed; Derieux Anne
source: Proceedings of the Asian Test Symposium
abstract: A new statistical method for analog fault simulation is presented. The method takes into account process parameter variations and aims to reduce the number of the computational expensive Monte Carlo simulations often required during analog fault simulation. The technique is illustrated by means of a fifth-order low-pass switched-capacitor filter.

title: Simulation-based test design for mixed-signal systems; [Simulationsbasierter Testentwurf für gemischt analog-digitale Systeme]
authors: Pronath M.; Glöckel V.; Gräb H.; Antreich K.
source: IT - Information Technology
abstract: Production test of complex embedded systems is difficult and expensive. Analog components are often the source. The performance test of these components requires very complex and expensive testers, and a test can last several minutes [1]. In this paper, power-supply current measurements, which are already used for digital testing, are used by the test design for analog components. The presented simulation- based test design method is based on deterministic and statistical methods and allows for inference from test measurements to specified performances. The test design method is evaluated by the simulation results of a CMOS OpAmp. © R. Oldenbourg Verlag.

title: Estimation of parameter fluctuations for robust operation in analogue circuits and systems
authors: Kadim H.J.; Harvey D.M.
source: Proceedings - IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems
abstract: The design of an analogue circuit consists of assigning values to a set of designed parameters so that the circuit meets design objectives while satisfying a set of performance specifications. Due to inherent fluctuations in IC manufacturing processes, manufactured circuits exhibit a spread in performance values. However, while a circuit's manufacturing yield is high it might be very sensitive to variations in environmental conditions such as power supply and temperature. Such sensitivity causes the circuit to have low operating performance. In this paper an estimation method of parameter fluctuations is proposed, based on analytical modelling equations, independent of simulation.
keywords: Integrated circuit layout; Mathematical models; Parameter estimation; Sensitivity analysis; Analog circuits; Linear integrated circuits

title: Fault detection method for the subcircuits of a cascade linear circuit
authors: Li F.; Woo P.-Y.
source: IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems I: Fundamental Theory and Applications
abstract: The fault detection method for the subcircuits of a cascade linear circuit is discussed. While there is any fault (either 'hard' or 'soft' and either 'single' or 'multiple') at one subcircuit of a cascade linear circuit, it can be quickly detected by using the method proposed in this brief. While there are faults simultaneously existing at multiple subcircuits, they can generally be detected by the searching approach proposed in this brief. The aforementioned method is the continuation and development of the unified fault detection dictionary method for linear circuits proposed in [1].
keywords: Computer aided network analysis; Electric admittance; Electric network parameters; Equivalent circuits; Sensitivity analysis; Cascade linear circuits; Fault detection method; Subcircuits; Linear networks

title: Fault simulation for analog circuits under parameter variations
authors: Khouas A.; Derieux A.
source: Journal of Electronic Testing: Theory and Applications (JETTA)
abstract: Analog integrated circuit testing and diagnosis is a very challenging problem. The inaccuracy of measurements, the infinite domain of possible values and the parameter deviations are among the major difficulties. During the process of optimizing production tests, Monte Carlo simulation is often needed due to parameter variations, but because of its expensive computational cost, it becomes the bottleneck of such a process. This paper describes a new technique to reduce the number of simulations required during analog fault simulation. This leads to the optimization of production tests subjected to parameter variations. In Section 1 a review of the state of the art is presented, Section 2 introduces the algorithm and describes the methodology of our approach. The results on CMOS 2-stage opamp and Fifth-order Low-pass switched-capacitor Filter are given in Sections 3 and conclusions in Section 4.
keywords: Algorithms; CMOS integrated circuits; Computer simulation; Digital filters; Linear integrated circuits; Normal distribution; Operational amplifiers; Probability density function; Analog testing; Fault simulation; Test optimization; Integrated circuit testing

title: An analogue test response compaction technique using delta-sigma modulation
authors: Saine S.; Raczkowycz J.; Mather P.
source: Microelectronics Journal
abstract: An analogue and mixed-signal Built-In-Self-Test (BIST) scheme suitable for detecting manufacturing defects in embedded linear macros is presented. The BIST scheme uses a delta-sigma (ΔΣ) modulator and a binary counter to perform an analogue test response compaction technique. This technique produces a signature for a circuit under test, which relates to the amplitude and frequency of the analogue response. Fault simulations performed on a two-stage CMOS operational amplifier and a continuous-time state variable filter have shown that a fault coverage (>80%) is attainable. These simulation results suggest that the probability of any fault masking occurring using the proposed compression technique is insignificant. © 2001 Published by Elsevier Science Ltd.
